title: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm
author: Nicole Seah

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s operating-model thesis and materially develops it through a specific neofirm model: legal-service providers sell outputs at fixed fees and reinvest corporate profits in R&D rather than relying on hourly billing and partnership distributions. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that judgment-intensive legal work remains difficult for AI to assess reliably, though its performance claims are predictive rather than comparatively demonstrated.
qs: Neo-firms eschew selling human time, and instead charge on outputs – a predictable fixed fee, as opposed to the unexpected final bill of a black-box process.

Crosby, and more broadly the hybrid institutions which will proliferate in the future, are corporations where profits don’t get doled out individually but are re-invested into R&D – continuing to make them faster, cheaper, and better.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI adoption is a business-model problem, contrasting hourly billing with output-based fixed fees. It materially extends the synthesis by proposing a specific corporate “neofirm” structure that reinvests profits in R&D rather than distributing them annually, while recognising that judgment-dependent legal work remains difficult to automate.
qs: Neo-firms eschew selling human time, and instead charge on outputs – a predictable fixed fee, as opposed to the unexpected final bill of a black-box process.

Crosby, and more broadly the hybrid institutions which will proliferate in the future, are corporations where profits don’t get doled out individually but are re-invested into R&D – continuing to make them faster, cheaper, and better.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI pressures hourly, labour-based legal production while legal judgment remains difficult to automate. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a specific neofirm model built around output-based fixed fees, corporate ownership and reinvestment in R&D, though its performance claims are predictive rather than independently demonstrated.
qs: Neo-firms eschew selling human time, and instead charge on outputs – a predictable fixed fee, as opposed to the unexpected final bill of a black-box process.

Crosby, and more broadly the hybrid institutions which will proliferate in the future, are corporations where profits don’t get doled out individually but are re-invested into R&D – continuing to make them faster, cheaper, and better.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment: AI can deliver large gains on bounded contract work, but legal judgment, trust and responsibility keep capable lawyers in the loop. It materially extends the proposition with a concrete neofirm operating model combining fixed-fee outputs, lawyer-led evaluation, legal-engineering roles, close lawyer-engineer feedback and operational forecasting, while acknowledging that its productivity evidence is controlled and execution may vary.
qs: If Tenzin Dolkar, one of the first lawyers at Crosby, had to use one word to describe the personality patterning at Crosby, she would use “awake.”  If the lawyers were initially scared of their job being automated away long term, it soon became clear that usage and trust relied on a high performing lawyer being in the loop.

Success probably means something more than just the best technology, but motivating and running a team of professionals that feel they have a stake in the future, with a sports team-like sense of drive to win.

st.t: AI contracting: Deal velocity can undermine negotiation
st.an: Seah supports the cluster’s core distinction between AI-native delivery and software sales, while treating speed gains as qualified rather than proof of quality-adjusted value. Her observed 10x NDA result is explicitly limited to a known sample and one contract type, and her emphasis on lawyer control, judgment and relational work reinforces that faster review cannot by itself establish better negotiation outcomes.
qs: They employ lawyers, own liability, and take on the work end to end.
That day the productivity lift was 10x, though in a sterile environment: a known sample, one contract type.

st.t: Contract automation: Owning delivery enables embedded feedback
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s characterization of Crosby as an organisational and service model rather than validated evidence of automation performance. Its anecdotal accounts reinforce the roles of complementary leadership, execution-focused culture, founder-oriented hiring and end-to-end service ambition, but do not demonstrate faster contracting or scalable automation.
qs: I sense the motivation is not making the most money or raising shiny capital, but building a seamless end to end service.
I want to hire people who are either like: this is my last job, or this is my second to last job because I’m starting a company after.

st.t: Crosby delivery: Owning work enables workflow redesign
st.an: Seah’s profile supports the service-delivery thesis by describing Crosby as owning liability and delivering contract work end to end, with AI accelerating workflows while lawyers retain control, judgment and client relationships. Its observed speed evidence is narrow, and it treats personalised agents and broader effects as ambitions rather than established capabilities.
qs: They employ lawyers, own liability, and take on the work end to end.
The team at Crosby is pretty opinionated that product choices really matter in preserving lawyer choice and agency.

kp.k: Immersive reporting provides a company-specific account
kp.d: Seah bases the account on two weeks inside Crosby, observing meetings and lawyers, and over 25 conversations, including interviews with investors and a customer. The account combines observed practices with company ambitions and interviewees’ views rather than presenting a market-wide study.
qs: This piece came together after over 25 conversations with the team and an immersive two weeks in their New York office in the heart of SoHo.

kp.k: Neofirms deliver legal work rather than merely software
kp.d: Crosby is described as an AI-native law firm combining lawyers and engineers, employing lawyers, assuming liability and delivering commercial-contract work end to end. Its scope includes NDAs and MSAs, with movement toward greater complexity. The article reports $85M raised and customers including Ramp, Cognition, Cursor and Clay.
qs: They call it a neofirm: equal parts lawyers from elite law firms like Kirkland and Ellis and Wachtell, and engineers from top startups like Ramp and Stripe.
They employ lawyers, own liability, and take on the work end to end.
They’ve raised $85M from Sequoia, Lux, Index, Elad Gil, BCV, and serve customers like Ramp, Cognition, Cursor, and Clay.

kp.k: Controlled redlining trials show bounded productivity gains
kp.d: Seah observed an AI-assisted NDA review completed in four minutes and fifty-three seconds; a team member supplied an approximately 58 min unaided comparison. She characterizes that day’s lift as 10x but expressly limits it to a known sample and one contract type, questioning real-world performance and trust. Internal trial records reportedly improved week after week as AI suggestions became more acceptable to lawyers.
qs: He finished the Non Disclosure Agreement in four minutes and fifty-three seconds with the help of an internal AI redlining harness.
Turns out, the same document would usually take a human lawyer with no technology around 58 min to complete.
That day the productivity lift was 10x, though in a sterile environment: a known sample, one contract type.

kp.k: Fixed fees and reinvestment challenge partnership economics
kp.d: Seah contrasts neofirms’ predictable output-based fixed fees with hourly billing and argues that corporate structures reinvest profits in R&D rather than distributing them to partners. She depicts traditional junior lawyers as costs to optimize with deliberately high turnover, and predicts proliferation of hybrid institutions. This is the author’s structural argument, not a demonstrated sector-wide transition.
qs: Neo-firms eschew selling human time, and instead charge on outputs – a predictable fixed fee, as opposed to the unexpected final bill of a black-box process.
Junior lawyers often feel like “operating expenses to be optimized,” and turnover is purposefully high.

Crosby, and more broadly the hybrid institutions which will proliferate in the future, are corporations where profits don’t get doled out individually but are re-invested into R&D – continuing to make them faster, cheaper, and better.

kp.k: Incumbents and foundation models constrain market opportunity
kp.d: Seah cautions that the market is not open territory for neofirms: foundation models threaten the legal application layer, while major incumbent firms are investing internally. She cites Kirkland & Ellis spending $500M on its own technology.
qs: The market is far from being wide open.
The foundation models threaten to erode the legal application layer entirely, and legacy firms like Kirkland & Ellis, one of the premier big law firms, are spending
building internal technology.

kp.k: Legal judgment complicates objective assessment of AI
kp.d: Seah frames law as a domain in which correctness depends on interpretation, drafting choices and changing client preferences, contrasting it with coding and mathematics. This motivates Crosby’s efforts to improve evaluation and encode context rather than assume a single correct redline.
qs: What counts as a ‘correct’ answer in law is open to interpretation.
Two smart lawyers might disagree about whether a specific edit in a document was necessary, or how to implement it.
Different things matter to different clients, who often change their minds.

kp.k: Custom evaluations turn lawyer feedback into product improvement
kp.d: The article reports online evaluations intended to detect regressions on generated edits, offline datasets incorporating failure cases, and lawyer-controlled tuning of judges and on-demand evaluations. Ross Weiser works on a playbook schema and an LLM-as-judge system comparing AI outputs with what reviewers actually sent. These are evaluation mechanisms, distinct from lawyers checking an individual contract before use.
qs: They created their own evaluation infrastructure, and have set up online evals to detect when a system has regressed on every edit that’s generated.
It allows lawyers to tune judges and be able to run evals on demand.
He’s currently working on a playbook schema for the eval system, and LLM as a judge system for grading Crosby’s AI outputs as compared against what a reviewer actually sent out.

kp.k: Living playbooks capture evolving client preferences
kp.d: Crosby is building systems that retain client instructions, including Slack messages, and company context in playbooks retrievable by humans and agents. Seah describes faster agreement through better modeling of priorities and compromises as a theoretical benefit, not a measured result.
qs: Client preferences and playbooks are hard to define ex ante, given they’re constantly evolving.
It remembers instructions a client gives Crosby in any format (e.g. Slack messages), keeps relevant context about a company, and creates a living, breathing, corpus of rules.
This theoretically gets clients to agreement faster by simulating accurately what a client cares about and is inversely willing to compromise on.

kp.k: Agentic delivery requires specialized infrastructure and capacity planning
kp.d: Crosby’s agents are described as long-running, stateful and costly to restart, motivating infrastructure for thousands of simultaneous contract reviews. Separately, its internal routing system uses predictive models of outages and seasonality to calculate supply and demand and guide customer growth while maintaining quality.
qs: They are long-running, stateful, and expensive to restart.
Their infra team builds to support large workloads of thousands of contracts being reviewed simultaneously.
They developed an in-house internal routing “brain” that calculates supply and demand based on predictive models of outages and seasonality.

kp.k: Autonomous review remains a research ambition
kp.d: Founding research engineer Sharan Ramjee presents custom reward models and reinforcement learning as a possible route to autonomous contract review. The team believes end-to-end service delivery provides negotiation-lifecycle and lawyer-evaluation data, but extracting counterparty preferences remains unresolved. Investor Grace Isford’s suggestion that Crosby could arbitrate negotiations across industries is explicitly a future belief.
qs: Through our research arm, the question we’re driving toward is how to turn contract review into a more verifiable domain by building custom reward models. Eventually, this can pave the way to autonomous review through reinforcement learning
Yet they’re the first to admit they haven’t figured it all out.
How do you actually understand and extract these different preferences from counterparties that we’ve negotiated against?

Grace Isford, the Series B lead investor in Crosby, believes that by pioneering non-verifiable reinforcement learning for contracts, Crosby can eventually become the arbiter of any type of negotiation across different industries.

kp.k: Client trust still depends on accountable human lawyers
kp.d: The account reports that use and trust require a high-performing lawyer in the loop despite initial fears of automation. Ross Weiser says clients still seek identifiable responsibility. Braintrust customer Sarah Zeng attributes confidence in migrating all contracts to cross-checking features, internal notes and estimated completion times; this is a customer’s reported experience, not general evidence of reliability.
qs: If the lawyers were initially scared of their job being automated away long term, it soon became clear that usage and trust relied on a high performing lawyer being in the loop.
They want to know that they can trust us. They want to know who’s responsible. It is just so human.

Sarah Zeng, the Chief of Staff at Braintrust, a customer of Crosby, told me “cross checking” features, detailed internal notes, and “estimated time of arrival” metrics were invaluable for giving them the confidence to migrate all of Braintrust’s contracts over.

kp.k: Lawyer roles expand into engineering and agent orchestration
kp.d: Weiser’s work illustrates a lawyer taking on legal-engineering responsibilities. Crosby’s team argues that product design can preserve professional agency by letting lawyers direct agents rather than become subordinate proofreaders. The prospect of lawyers encoding expertise, client preferences and negotiation styles into scalable agent versions remains an imagined future.
qs: Now he works in the new multi-hyphenated role of legal engineering.
In aggregate you can either make the lawyers feel like they are at the service of a robot or they are in control, directing them and orchestrating.
It’s very intoxicating to find leverage on productivity rather than just proofreading which feels reductive or commoditized.

kp.k: Automation could increase relational and expert work
kp.d: Seah argues that strong negotiators retain high value by allocating risk in ways acceptable to both parties. Crosby’s aspirational lawyer workplace combines intellectually difficult expert work with reasonable hours; Bijan Motiwalla links end-to-end client relationships to ownership of trust. Seah’s conclusion that less routine work could make legal work more relational is conditional, not a finding about long-term employment outcomes.
qs: The best lawyers move from being transactional to integrative, allocating risk to both parties in a way that makes them both feel like they’ve won.
They only do expert work, solving intellectually tricky problems, while working reasonable hours.
If you own the relationship end to end, you own trust.

If lawyers can spend less time on deadweight tasks, their time becomes *even more* relational - building mutual context and trust between strangers, where the process of getting to an agreement is an end in itself.

kp.k: Close collaboration exposes tacit legal reasoning
kp.d: Engineer Anthony Corletti describes learning through extended observation of Ryan’s redlining, including why avoiding unnecessary language can facilitate counterparty acceptance. Seah presents routine shadowing, physical proximity and experimentation as mechanisms for translating lawyers’ tacit judgments into technical improvements.
qs: Shadowing is a practice in everyday empathy.
Because when we send this contract back, we would like them to say accept all or this is okay, deal is closed. It was unintuitive. You learn so much watching the lawyers work.
Tight feedback loops happen when lawyers and engineers literally sit next to each other in the office rather than in an ivory tower.

kp.k: Traditional junior safeguards can restrict learning
kp.d: Ryan Daniels recalls junior practice that prohibited direct document editing and allowed only handwritten changes. He acknowledges the error-prevention rationale but describes the arrangement as belittling and questions how juniors can learn under such restrictions. This is a personal account of traditional formation, not evidence that Crosby has solved AI-era training.
qs: No, you can’t even edit the document. You can just write on it with a pen. It was kinda belittling.
It did make everything failproof, because the most likely person to make a mistake is the junior associate.
But I was just like: How am I going to learn?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Seah presents AI-native legal services as a combination of faster contract work, output-based pricing, integrated legal and engineering work, and continuing human responsibility; interviewees envision eventual autonomous review and broader negotiation services.
pts.d: Seah reports an approximately tenfold productivity improvement in a controlled NDA redlining exercise using Crosby's internal AI harness. She attributes improving review speeds to increasingly precise AI suggestions that lawyers accept more readily. She describes Crosby as an end-to-end legal-service provider employing lawyers and assuming liability, rather than merely selling software. Her business-model argument is that neofirms charge predictable fixed fees for outputs and reinvest corporate profits in R&D, enabling further improvements in speed, cost and quality; she predicts that such hybrid institutions will proliferate. She also identifies competitive pressure from foundation models and incumbent law firms' internal technology investments. Crosby's team believes delivering services directly supplies negotiation-lifecycle data and lawyer-evaluation data that improve its systems. Seah describes evolving client-preference playbooks as a potential way to accelerate agreement. Founding Research Engineer Sharan Ramjee envisages custom reward models making contract review more verifiable and eventually enabling autonomous review through reinforcement learning. Investor Grace Isford predicts possible expansion into negotiation across industries. The team's further aspirations include agents encoding individual lawyers' expertise and negotiation styles. These future ambitions coexist with the current human-in-the-loop model: Ross Weiser reports clients' continuing demand for accountable people, while Seah predicts that skilled negotiation and relational advice will retain high value. She describes lawyers moving into legal engineering and evaluation work, and presents agent orchestration, expert-only work and reasonable hours as an aspirational alternative to repetitive proofreading.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source rests on immersive observation, internal timing records, interviews and customer testimony; its longer-term predictions are attributed ambitions rather than demonstrated results.
pts.d: Seah bases the account on two weeks inside Crosby and more than 25 conversations, including staff, investors and a customer. She personally observes an AI-assisted NDA review completed in four minutes and fifty-three seconds; the approximately 58-minute unaided comparison comes from a team member, not a separately observed control in the account. Product lead Amy Danoff supplies internal time-trial records with notes, which Seah says show substantial week-to-week improvements. These are internal timing exercises, not an independent benchmark of legal accuracy or market-wide productivity. The article describes online and offline evaluation infrastructure, failure-case collection, lawyer-tuned judges and comparisons between model output and what reviewers actually sent. These descriptions explain the proposed improvement mechanism but provide no numerical legal-quality results. Braintrust Chief of Staff Sarah Zeng supplies customer testimony that cross-checking features, internal notes and delivery estimates supported confidence in moving all of its contracts to Crosby. Lawyer interviews support claims about trust, accountability, changing work and agency. Predictions about autonomous review, cross-industry negotiation and neofirm proliferation are based on research goals, investor expectations and Seah's interpretation of the field study rather than reported demonstrations of those future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current observations concern supervised commercial-contract work; autonomy, wider negotiation capabilities and occupational transformation have no specified delivery dates and depend on unresolved technical and organisational conditions.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026 account, Crosby already handles commercial contracts, including NDAs and MSAs, and is moving toward greater complexity. The tenfold speed claim is explicitly restricted to a known sample and a single contract type in a controlled setting; Seah asks whether it will hold in real-world work. She presents legal judgment as difficult to evaluate because reasonable lawyers disagree and client preferences change. Autonomous review is an eventual possibility conditional on research into custom reward models and reinforcement learning, not a description of current autonomous delivery. More effective repeated negotiations depend on extracting evolving client and counterparty preferences, a problem CTO John Sarihan says remains unresolved. Trust must accumulate among both customers and lawyers. The envisioned improvement in lawyers' working lives depends on product choices that preserve agency and on motivating professionals, rather than on technology alone; Seah says not all neofirms will succeed at this. She explicitly disclaims certainty about the long-term form of legal work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected groups are business clients buying commercial-contract services, lawyers and engineers delivering them, and incumbent firms competing with AI-native providers.
pts.d: Business clients are offered faster contract processing, predictable output-based fees, retained preference context, delivery visibility and accountable human advisers; the article names technology-company customers including Ramp, Cognition, Cursor, Clay and Braintrust. Crosby's lawyers may shift from repetitive redlining toward negotiation, relationship ownership, supervising agents and building evaluation systems. Ross Weiser exemplifies a qualified lawyer taking on legal-engineering responsibilities; this is a role change, not evidence that legal engineers generally must be lawyers. An unnamed lawyer contrasts empowering agent orchestration with reductive proofreading, while Bijan Motiwalla links end-to-end client relationship ownership to trust. Engineers and operations staff become integrated participants in service delivery, with shared feedback loops and workload-routing infrastructure. Traditional partnerships and junior lawyers are affected in Seah's contrast between time-selling, partner distributions and high turnover versus corporate R&D reinvestment, but she supplies no quantified displacement or hiring forecast. The article gestures toward similar changes for bankers, consultants and doctors without providing comparable domain-specific evidence. Its client benefits concern enterprise legal services, not evidence of closing the civil access-to-justice gap.
